hints: Treat each row as two tests, the property must be true and the explanation must correctly explain it, so check the fact first.
Recall which silver halide dissolves in dilute ammonia, and recall that $\text{HI}$ with its longer, weaker bond decomposes far more easily than $\text{HCl}$.
Compare $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{Cl}_2$ for number of electrons and size to predict van der Waals forces, then remember oxidising power increases up Group 17.
walkthrough:
**Check Row A, solubility in ammonia**

Think of the classic test. $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia to give the complex ion, but $\text{AgBr}$ needs concentrated ammonia and $\text{AgI}$ is insoluble.

$$\text{AgCl} + 2\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+ + \text{Cl}^-$$

**Check Row B, thermal stability of hydrogen halides**

Stability decreases down Group 17 because the $\text{H-X}$ bond gets longer and weaker. So $\text{HI}$ decomposes much more readily than $\text{HCl}$, not the other way round.

Bond strength: $\text{H-Cl} > \text{H-I}$, so the property statement is backwards.

**Check Row C, melting point of halogens**

Both $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{Cl}_2$ are simple covalent molecules, so melting depends on London (van der Waals) forces between molecules.

$$\text{I}_2 \text{ has more electrons and a larger electron cloud than } \text{Cl}_2$$

**Link size to forces and finish with Row D**

A larger cloud is more easily polarised, so $\text{I}_2$ has stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces and a higher melting point. Solid $\text{I}_2$ versus gaseous $\text{Cl}_2$ confirms this.

Row D is backwards too, $\text{Cl}_2$ is the stronger oxidising agent because Cl gains electrons more readily up the group.

options.A: False. The property is wrong. $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves readily in dilute aqueous ammonia, while $\text{AgI}$ does not dissolve. The trap is reversing the solubility trend, solubility in ammonia decreases from chloride to iodide.
options.B: False. The property is reversed. $\text{HI}$ decomposes more readily than $\text{HCl}$ because the $\text{H-I}$ bond is longer and weaker. Electronegativity of Cl is true but it does not explain decomposition, bond enthalpy does.
options.C: Correct. Both parts are true and linked. $\text{I}_2$ has more electrons than $\text{Cl}_2$, so it has stronger London van der Waals forces between molecules, requiring more energy to separate them and giving a higher melting point.
options.D: False. The property is reversed. $\text{Cl}_2$ is a stronger oxidising agent than $\text{I}_2$, oxidising power decreases down Group 17. An I atom losing electrons more readily would make $\text{I}_2$ a better reducing agent, not a better oxidising agent.
